original_value: Heart rate variability (HRV), using electrocardiography (ECG), has gained popularity as a biomarker of the stress response. Alternatives to HRV monitoring, like photoplethysmography (PPG), are being explored as cheaper and unobtrusive non-invasive technologies. We report a new wireless PPG sensor that was tested in detecting changes in HRV, elicited by a mentally stressful task, and to determine if its signal can be used as a surrogate of ECG for HRV analysis. Data were collected simultaneously from volunteers using a PPG and ECG sensor, during a resting and a mentally stressful task. HRV metrics were extracted from these signals and compared to determine the agreement between them and to determine if any changes occurred in the metrics due to the stressful task. For both tasks, a moderate/good agreement was found in the mean interbeat intervals, SDNN, LF, and SD2, and a poor agreement for the pNN50, RMSSD|SD1, and HF metrics. The majority of the tested HRV metrics obtained from the PPG signal showed a significant decrease caused by the mental task. The disagreement found between specific HRV features imposes caution when comparing metrics from different technologies. Nevertheless, the tested sensor was successful at detecting changes in the HRV caused by a mental stressor.

result.paraphrase: Heart rate variability (HRV), measured with electrocardiography (ECG), has become a widely used biomarker of the stress response. As lower-cost, unobtrusive non-invasive alternatives to HRV monitoring, technologies such as photoplethysmography (PPG) are being investigated. Here, we present a new wireless PPG sensor that was evaluated for detecting HRV changes induced by a mentally stressful task and for assessing whether its signal can serve as a surrogate for ECG in HRV analysis. Simultaneous data were collected from volunteers using PPG and ECG sensors during both a resting condition and a mentally stressful task. HRV metrics were extracted and compared to assess agreement between the two signals and to determine whether the stressful task altered any metrics. For both tasks, moderate to good agreement was observed for mean interbeat intervals, SDNN, LF, and SD2, whereas pNN50, RMSSD|SD1, and HF showed poor agreement. Most HRV metrics derived from the PPG signal decreased significantly in response to the mental task. The disagreement observed for certain HRV features indicates that caution is needed when comparing metrics across different technologies. Nonetheless, the tested sensor successfully detected HRV changes caused by mental stress.
